pages.name: Introduction
pages.subtitle: HOW TO USE THIS BOOK
pages.html:
Introduction

Reading must begin early in the life of a child, whether it is just an alphabet letter, a word, a sentence, a paragraph, or a story. Teaching children how to read must begin early on, and children should be exposed to books, stories, rhymes, and be read to on a daily basis.

This book provides the practice you need to improve your spelling and writing ability and to expand your vocabulary. Each spelling lesson focuses on a single spelling pattern or concept that applies to a list of words in a Word Store.

We've also introduced the Phonics Primer from the National Right to Read Foundation (www.nrrf.org) to help Teachers and Parents understand the steps and methods of teaching the 44 sounds of the English language.

How Each Unit Works
  • Word Store — the list of spelling words for the unit.
  • Key Ideas — the pattern explained in plain language.
  • Word Sort — grouping words by sound or spelling.
  • Word Meaning — matching words to definitions.
  • Proofreading — finding and correcting misspelled words.
  • Phonetic & Decoding Skills — proving words.

pages.html:
Steps For Teaching Phonics
Step 1. Teach the 5 short-vowel sounds and consonant sounds. Drill until memorized.

During the first week, use the flash cards to drill the short-vowel sounds. Add several consonant sounds each day until you are drilling all short-vowel sounds and consonant sounds with your student daily. Do not rush this step. Keep drilling until all sounds are memorized, which usually takes 2–4 weeks.

Tip: Work on phonics for at least 15 minutes a day, 5 days a week with your student. Frequency and consistency are more important than the length of time spent on each lesson.

pages.name: Steps 2 & 3 — Blends
pages.subtitle: TWO-LETTER & THREE-LETTER BLENDS
pages.html:
Step 2 & Step 3
Step 2. Practice two-letter blends. Drill until blending is automatic.

After your student knows the short-vowel sounds and consonant sounds, next teach him how to orally blend two letters (b-a, ba) and read two-letter blends such as: ba, be, bi, bo, bu.

Two-Letter Blends
b + a = bas + a = sai + a = ia
b + e = bes + e = sei + e = ie
b + i = bis + i = sii + i = ii
b + o = bos + o = soi + o = io
b + u = bus + u = sui + u = iu
Step 3. Practice three-letter blends. Drill until blending is automatic.

After your student can read two-letter blends, progress to three-letter blends, that is, words.

Golden Rule of Phonics: Never allow your student to skip, guess, or substitute words. Accuracy is more important than speed.
Three-Letter Blends
fa + t = fatki + t = kitro + d = rod
de + n = denma + d = madse + t = set
bo + x = boxve + s = vestu + g = tug
hi + d = hidno + t = notwi + n = win
ju + g = jugpu + n = punla + p = lap

pages.name: Steps 12–14
pages.subtitle: STORIES · BOOKS · SPELLING
pages.html:
Steps 12–14
Step 12. After 3 to 4 months of daily phonics instruction, begin introducing decodable stories.

All sounds and spellings in Steps 1–11 should be introduced within the first 4 months of phonics instruction. The student should read all stories aloud, carefully and accurately.

Step 13. Begin introducing "easy-to-read" books.

Dr. Seuss, P. D. Eastman, Cynthia Rylant and others. Continue teaching the lessons in the phonics program — don't stop just because your student can read. Most children need 1 to 2 years of reinforcement.

Step 14. Continue to give phonetically based spelling lists.

Even after your student has finished the phonics program, make sure to reinforce his phonics knowledge by giving phonetically based spelling lists each week at least through third grade.

Synthetic Phonics Instruction

Before your child can learn to read, he or she must first learn some basic letter names and letter sounds. For example, the letter "A" makes the /a/ (ah) sound. To be able to read, a child must be able to recognize the letters, know the sound of the letters, and be able to recognize the letters quickly and say the sound without hesitation.

Always teach the letter name and letter sound together. Never separately. Studies have found that children receiving letter name and sound instruction were most likely to learn the sounds of letters whose names included cues to their sounds.

pages.name: Phonemic Awareness
pages.subtitle: NOTES
pages.html:
Developing Phonemic Awareness

Most people know or have heard of phonics, but not everyone knows what phonemic awareness (PA) is, and PA is one of the most important skills to develop in the process of learning to read.

Phonemic Awareness is defined as the ability to identify, hear, and work with the smallest units of sound known as phonemes. PA deals with phonemes and manipulating the individual sounds of words — such as /c/, /a/, and /t/ are the individual sounds that make up the word "cat".

Studies have found that phonemic awareness is the best predictor of reading success in young children. Research has also found that children with a high level of phonemic awareness progress with high reading and spelling achievements.

Blending Practice

Start blending practice with some ear training with your child. For example, if you wanted to ask your child to call his mother, you could say: "Aseda, call your mmmmaaammmaa." The word mama is sounded out slowly and "stretchily."

Key Ideas
  • A blend is two or three consonants whose sounds flow together: splash, strong, brush, plant, thread, cream, frost, glass, twist, stamp.
  • A digraph is two consonants that form one new sound: chick, thorn, whisper, shrimp, thank, th (in month).
  • In blends you hear every letter. In digraphs the two letters make a single sound.

Answer Key — Word Sort (cont.)
Notes on Sort Criteria
Different patterns use different sorting criteria. Use the criterion that genuinely divides the words into meaningful groups:
• Spelling-letter grouping (Units 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14): sort by which letter or letters spell the target sound.
• Alphabetical order (Units 3, 4, 8, 9): used when the words share the same sound or rule and cannot be split into meaningful sound groups. This also teaches dictionary skills.
• Word analysis (Units 12, 15, 16): sort by which suffix or spelling rule applies.

pages.name: Glossary
pages.subtitle: KEY TERMS
pages.html:
Glossary
TermMeaning
BlendTwo or three consonants whose sounds flow together (splash, strong).
ConsonantAny letter of the alphabet other than a, e, i, o, u.
DecodingUsing knowledge of letter sounds to read a word.
DigraphTwo letters that together make one new sound (ch, sh, th).
DiphthongTwo vowels that make a new sound when combined (oi, ow).
Long vowelA vowel that says its own name (cake, feet, pie, boat, mule).
PhonemeThe smallest unit of sound in a word.
PhonicsA method of teaching reading that links letters to sounds.
ProofreadTo read and correct errors in writing.
r-controlled vowelA vowel followed by r where the sound changes (park, fork, fern).
SchwaAn unstressed vowel sound, heard as a soft "uh".
Short vowelA vowel with a short sound (apple, egg, igloo, octopus, umbrella).
Silent letterA letter that is written but not pronounced (knock, island).
SuffixA group of letters added to the end of a word (-ing, -ful, -ment).
SyllableA unit of sound in a word containing one vowel sound.
Word StoreThe list of spelling words for a unit.
